summary: Defines the Network Control Protocol for setting up and configuring IPX over PPP. It was a standards-track specification. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1552 defines IPXCP, the part of PPP that sets up Novell's IPX protocol on a point-to-point link. After the link itself is configured, the two ends exchange messages to agree on the network number, node number, compression and routing details. Only when that negotiation finishes can IPX datagrams be sent.

questions: what is ppp network control protocol
subtitle: How two ends of a PPP link agree on the settings needed to carry Novell IPX traffic.

tldr.problem: PPP can carry several network-layer protocols, but each one needs its own settings, such as a network number and a node number, agreed before any traffic flows.
tldr.mechanism: IPXCP is a network control protocol that runs after PPP has configured the link. It uses the same packet exchange as the Link Control Protocol, with a distinct set of configuration options covering the network number, node number, compression protocol, routing protocol, router name and a completion flag.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1552 is Historic and the RFC Editor recommends it for no further use. It was a standards track specification, and it records that Novell's own implementation, which used IPXCP with no configuration options at all, could not interoperate with implementations that did not already support IPX-WAN.

today: RFC 1552 is Historic, which means the RFC Editor recommends it for no further use. It was written as a standards track specification of the PPP network control protocol for IPX and has not been obsoleted by a later RFC.

sections.title: Where IPXCP Fits in PPP
sections.content:
PPP has three main components: a method for encapsulating multi-protocol datagrams, a Link Control Protocol for establishing, configuring and testing the data-link connection, and a family of Network Control Protocols for establishing and configuring different network-layer protocols.

To establish communications over a point-to-point link, each end must first send LCP packets to configure and test the data link. After the link has been established and optional facilities have been negotiated as needed by the LCP, PPP must send IPXCP packets to choose and configure the IPX network-layer protocol. Once IPXCP has reached the Opened state, IPX datagrams can be sent over the link. The link stays configured until explicit LCP or IPXCP packets close it down, or until an external event occurs, such as an inactivity timer expiring or network administrator intervention.

The memo uses the usual requirement keywords: MUST and MUST NOT for absolute requirements, SHOULD where there may be valid reasons to ignore an item but the implications should be weighed, and MAY for one of an allowed set of alternatives, where an implementation that does not include the option must be prepared to interoperate with one that does. It also defines the terms peer, the other end of the link, silently discard, meaning to drop a packet without further processing while logging the error and counting it, end-system, a user's machine that only sends packets to servers and other end-systems and does not pass packets through itself, router, which passes packets through, usually from one Ethernet segment to another, and half-router, two normal routers joined by an unnumbered link, each made to look like a single machine because NetWare does not understand unnumbered links.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP has three parts: a way to wrap different kinds of packet, a link control protocol that brings the line up and tests it, and one network control protocol per network-layer protocol. IPXCP is the one for Novell's IPX. Nothing IPX-related can be sent until the link is up and IPXCP has finished negotiating.

sections.title: How IPXCP Differs from the Link Control Protocol
sections.content:
The IPX Control Protocol is responsible for configuring, enabling and disabling the IPX protocol modules on both ends of the link. IPXCP uses the same packet exchange mechanism as the Link Control Protocol, and IPXCP packets may not be exchanged until PPP has reached the Network-Layer Protocol phase; IPXCP packets received before that phase is reached should be silently discarded.

The protocol is exactly the same as the Link Control Protocol with four exceptions. The packet may use any modifications to the basic frame format that were negotiated during the Link Establishment phase. Exactly one IPXCP packet is encapsulated in the Information field of a PPP Data Link Layer frame whose Protocol field indicates type hex 802B, the IPX Control Protocol. Only Codes 1 through 7 are used, namely Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, Configure-Reject, Terminate-Request, Terminate-Ack and Code-Reject; other Codes should be treated as unrecognised and should result in Code-Rejects. Finally, an implementation should be prepared to wait for Authentication and Link Quality Determination to finish before timing out waiting for a Configure-Ack or other response, and it is suggested that an implementation give up only after user intervention or a configurable amount of time.

Before any IPX packets may be communicated, PPP must reach the Network-Layer Protocol phase and the IPX Control Protocol must reach the Opened state. Exactly one IPX packet is encapsulated in the Information field of a PPP Data Link Layer frame whose Protocol field indicates type hex 002B, an IPX datagram. The maximum length of an IPX datagram transmitted over a PPP link is the same as the maximum length of the Information field of a PPP data link layer frame. Since there is no standard method for fragmenting and reassembling IPX datagrams, PPP links supporting IPX must allow at least 576 octets in the information field of a data link layer frame.
sections.plainLanguage: IPXCP works the same way as the link control protocol, with three differences: it runs at a later stage of the link, it has its own packet type number, and it has its own set of options. It also sets a floor on the link: at least 576 bytes of payload per frame, because IPX datagrams cannot be split up and put back together again.

sections.title: Desired Parameters and Co-existence with IPX-WAN
sections.content:
A Novell specification called IPX-WAN provides mechanisms similar to IPXCP negotiation over wide area links. As viewed by PPP, IPX-WAN is a part of IPX, and IPX-WAN packets are indistinguishable from other IPX packets. The memo records that Novell had implemented IPXCP without any configuration options, and requires successful IPX-WAN completion even when all required parameters have been hand configured, which makes it impossible for the current Novell products to interoperate with other IPXCP implementations that do not already include support for IPX-WAN.

To resolve the possible conflict between the two configuration methods, the memo defines the concept of Desired Parameters. Where applicable, each configuration option indicates the environment in which the parameter being negotiated may be required by the implementation for proper operation. This determination is highly implementation dependent: a particular implementation might require that all links have addresses, while another might not need such addresses. The configuration negotiation is intended to discover that this pair of implementations will never converge.

An IPXCP implementation that includes support for IPX-WAN should always reach the Opened state, even when unable to negotiate some Desired Parameter and when no configuration options are successfully negotiated, which allows IPX-WAN the opportunity to finish the negotiation. An implementation that does not include support for IPX-WAN should not reach the Opened state in that situation. IPX-WAN uses a Timer Request packet to set up the link, and these must not be sent until IPXCP has opened the link. An implementation that provides both IPX-WAN and IPXCP configuration options capability should only send a Timer Request packet when a Timer Request packet is received, or upon failure to successfully negotiate a Desired Parameter. If unable to complete IPX-WAN setup when a Desired Parameter is unknown, IPXCP should by default terminate the link, though some implementations might be capable of operating without all indicated Desired Parameters, in which case the termination must be configurable.
sections.plainLanguage: Novell had a separate way of setting up IPX over wide area links, called IPX-WAN, and the two ways of doing the same job could conflict. The memo resolves this by letting each end declare a Desired Parameter, a setting it says it cannot work without. If the two ends need different things, the negotiation is expected to notice that and fail early rather than at the first packet.

sections.title: The Six Configuration Options
sections.content:
IPXCP configuration options allow modifications to the standard characteristics of the network-layer protocol to be negotiated. If an option is not included in a Configure-Request packet, the default value for that option is assumed. IPXCP uses the same configuration option format defined for the LCP, with a separate set of options. Up-to-date values of the IPXCP Option Type field are given in the most recent Assigned Numbers RFC. The current values are 1 IPX-Network-Number, 2 IPX-Node-Number, 3 IPX-Compression-Protocol, 4 IPX-Routing-Protocol, 5 IPX-Router-Name and 6 IPX-Configuration-Complete.

IPX-Network-Number negotiates the IPX network number to be used for the link, so that an implementation can learn the number or ensure agreement on it. The network number must be unique within the routing domain, or zero to indicate that it is not used for routing. Both ends of the link must have the same network number; when a Configure-Request is received with a lower network number than the one locally configured, a Configure-Nak must be returned with the highest network number. The field is four octets, and the option has a length of 6.

IPX-Node-Number negotiates the IPX node number for the local end of the link. The node number must be unique for the network number. The field is six octets and the option has a length of 8. It is a Desired Parameter when the implementation is operating as an end-system, and when the node number has been statically configured the option should not be negotiated unless requested by the peer.

IPX-Compression-Protocol negotiates the use of a specific compression protocol; by default compression is not enabled. The field is two octets and odd values are always the same as the PPP Data Link Layer Protocol field values for that same compression protocol, while even values are used when the compression protocol is interleaved with IPX packets. The values assigned are 0002 for Telebit Compressed IPX and 0235 for Shiva Compressed NCP/IPX. The option length is 4 or more.

IPX-Routing-Protocol negotiates the use of a specific routing protocol, or no routing protocol if desired. Multiple protocols may be requested by sending multiple options, and the no routing protocol required value is mutually exclusive with other values. By default, Novell's combination of Routing Information Protocol and Server Advertising Protocol is expected. The values are 0 for no routing protocol required, 1 reserved, 2 for Novell RIP/SAP required and 4 for Novell NLSP required. The field is two octets, sent most significant octet first, and the option length is 4 or more.

IPX-Router-Name conveys information about the IPX server name. Its nature is advisory only, it exists to improve the end system's ability to provide a simple user interface, and it must not be included in a Configure-Nak. The name should be between 1 and 47 ASCII characters long, using the characters A through Z, underscore, hyphen and the at sign, and on reception it should be padded to 48 characters with the NUL character. The option length is 3 or more. IPX-Configuration-Complete indicates that all implementation-dependent Desired Parameters are satisfied, which is a way of detecting when convergence will occur in a heterogeneous environment; it is advisory only and must not be included in a Configure-Nak. Its length is 2.
sections.plainLanguage: Six options can be negotiated. Two of them give the link its IPX network number and node number, which identify the link and the machine on the other end. Two more choose how the link compresses its traffic and which routing protocol runs over it. The fifth passes the name of the machine, and the sixth says that everything the link needs has been agreed, so the two ends can skip the slower Novell setup procedure.

sections.title: Measuring Link Delay and Throughput
sections.content:
The appendix notes the concern over correctly estimating the link delay, in units of 55 millisecond ticks, used by Novell routing protocols. IPX-WAN uses its Timer Request and Reply for this purpose, but the measured delay is multiplied by a factor of 6, because the measurement is made during initialisation of the link and does not reflect actual loading. The delay is better measured using the PPP LCP Echo facility, by inserting a timestamp in the data part of the Request and comparing it with the same timer when the reply returns, and this method could be used to periodically re-evaluate the actual round trip delay as link and system loads change. The echo packet size should be 576, to match the default IPX packet size.

In the absence of such dynamic measurements, empirical evidence has shown the following to be sufficient: 134 ticks at 2,400 bps, 21 ticks at 14,400 bps, 5 ticks at 57,600 bps and 1 tick above 1 Mbps.
sections.plainLanguage: Novell's routing protocols measure delay in ticks of 55 milliseconds, and the built-in measurement is taken while the link is being set up, so it does not reflect later load. The appendix suggests timing the link's own echo packets instead, and gives fixed values to use when that is not possible: 134 ticks on a 2,400 bit per second link, down to one tick on a link faster than 1 megabit per second.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo has a Security Considerations section, and its entire content is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.

Nothing in the document describes authentication or access control for the options it defines, beyond the rules already given for which options may appear in a Configure-Nak and which may be written by a manager.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss security. Its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed, so nothing in it should be read as a claim that the negotiation is protected.

messages.label: CONFIGURE-REQUEST
messages.note: End A offers its configuration options.

messages.label: CONFIGURE-ACK
messages.note: End B accepts the options as offered.

messages.label: CONFIGURE-NAK
messages.note: Instead of an acknowledgement, End B proposes different values.

messages.label: CONFIGURE-REJECT
messages.note: Or End B rejects an option it cannot accept.

messages.label: TERMINATE-REQUEST
messages.note: Either end may close the link.

messages.label: TERMINATE-ACK
messages.note: The other end confirms the close.

items.label: IPX-Network-Number
items.desc: A four octet network number for the link. Length 6.

items.label: IPX-Node-Number
items.desc: A six octet node number for the local end. Length 8.

items.label: IPX-Compression-Protocol
items.desc: Two octets naming the compression protocol. Length 4 or more.

items.label: IPX-Routing-Protocol
items.desc: Two octets naming the routing protocol, or none. Length 4 or more.

items.label: IPX-Router-Name
items.desc: The name of the IPX entity at this end, 1 to 47 characters. Length 3 or more.

items.label: IPX-Configuration-Complete
items.desc: Says all Desired Parameters are satisfied. Length 2.
